title: Illinois Civics & Constitution (8th Grade)
description: Illinois Civics & Constitution (8th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: According to the Declaration of Independence, governments are created mainly to do what?
questions.correctAnswer: Protect the natural rights of the people
questions.explanation: The Declaration says governments are instituted among men to secure their unalienable rights - protecting rights is the whole point of government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government's job is to guard your rights.

img.title: WHY GOVERNMENT EXISTS
img.tip: Government exists to protect the rights of the people.
img.scene: A stately government building with white columns and citizens gathered peacefully on its steps on a sunny day, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which document states that 'all men are created equal' and have unalienable rights?
questions.correctAnswer: The Declaration of Independence
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence, adopted in 1776, opens with the idea that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Equality and rights are the Declaration's opening promise.

img.title: CREATED EQUAL
img.tip: The Declaration of Independence announces equality and unalienable rights.
img.scene: An old parchment document resting on a wooden desk beside a quill and inkwell in warm light, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: In the Declaration of Independence, the long list of complaints is directed at whom?
questions.correctAnswer: King George III of Great Britain
distractors: The British Parliament as a whole
questions.explanation: Most of the Declaration is a list of grievances against King George III, showing the colonists' case that he had violated their rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The complaints point at one man - the king.

img.title: GRIEVANCES AGAINST A KING
img.tip: The Declaration lists the colonists' grievances against King George III.
img.scene: A stern king in a red royal robe and crown standing before a throne in a palace hall, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'consent of the governed' mean?
questions.correctAnswer: The government's power comes from the permission of the people it governs
distractors: The government may rule however it wishes
Only landowners may vote on laws
The king agrees to follow Parliament
questions.explanation: The Declaration teaches that governments get their just powers from the consent of the governed - the people are the source of authority.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Power flows upward, from the people.

img.title: CONSENT OF THE GOVERNED
img.tip: Just power comes from the consent of the people.
img.scene: A diverse crowd of citizens raising hands together in a town square in front of a public building, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which three rights does the Declaration of Independence name as unalienable?
questions.correctAnswer: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
questions.explanation: The Declaration names life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness as unalienable rights - rights that cannot be taken away.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life, liberty, happiness - the famous trio.

img.title: THREE UNALIENABLE RIGHTS
img.tip: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness cannot be taken away.
img.scene: Three tall candles burning brightly on a wooden table in a dark colonial room, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: In what year was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.explanation: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1776 - the birthday of the United States.

img.title: BORN IN 1776
img.tip: The Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776.
img.scene: Colonial townspeople celebrating in a 1776 street scene with flags and a liberty bell, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: The Declaration calls its key ideas 'self-evident' truths. What does self-evident mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Obviously true, needing no proof
distractors: Decided by a vote of Congress
questions.explanation: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident' means the truths are clear and obvious on their face - they do not need to be proven.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Self-evident means you can see it is true at once.

img.title: SELF-EVIDENT TRUTHS
img.tip: Self-evident truths are so clear they need no proof.
img.scene: Bright morning sunlight breaking over a colonial town square as people look up, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: According to the Declaration, what may the people do when a government keeps destroying their rights?
questions.correctAnswer: Alter it or abolish it and create a new government
distractors: Ask the king for permission to leave
Stop paying for public schools only
questions.explanation: The Declaration says that when government becomes destructive of rights, the people have the right to alter or abolish it and institute new government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rights-destroying government can be replaced by the people.

img.title: THE PEOPLE'S REMEDY
img.tip: A rights-destroying government may be altered or abolished by the people.
img.scene: Colonial citizens firmly rolling up a large broken chain on the ground near a harbor, symbolic historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: In what year was the United States Constitution written?
questions.explanation: Delegates at the Philadelphia Convention wrote the Constitution in 1787; it took effect in 1789.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1787 Philadelphia - the Constitution is drafted.

img.title: WRITTEN IN 1787
img.tip: The Constitution was written at Philadelphia in 1787.
img.scene: Delegates in colonial dress seated around long tables debating in a large hall with tall windows, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What do the first three words of the Constitution, 'We the People,' tell us?
questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution's authority comes from the people, not from a king or from the states alone
distractors: Only property owners wrote the Constitution
The President is the source of all law
Each state keeps its own separate constitution supreme
questions.explanation: 'We the People of the United States' announces popular sovereignty: the people themselves establish the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three little words put the people in charge.

img.title: WE THE PEOPLE
img.tip: Authority begins with the people themselves.
img.scene: A large diverse crowd of Americans of many ages standing together under a bright sky, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is the Constitution's position in the American legal system?
questions.correctAnswer: It is the supreme law of the land
distractors: It is advice that states may ignore
It applies only to the federal courts
questions.explanation: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution the supreme law of the land; no state or federal law may override it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Constitution sits at the very top.

img.title: SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND
img.tip: No law in America outranks the Constitution.
img.scene: A stone pyramid with a glowing book resting at its peak above smaller stone blocks, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many articles does the Constitution have?
questions.correctAnswer: Seven articles
questions.explanation: The Constitution's main body has seven articles. Its 27 amendments are separate additions, not articles.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Seven articles build the frame; amendments come later.

img.title: SEVEN ARTICLES
img.tip: The Constitution's main body is organized into seven articles.
img.scene: A large open book with seven ribbon bookmarks resting on a wooden desk, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many amendments does the Constitution have in total?
questions.correctAnswer: 27 amendments
questions.explanation: Since 1789 the Constitution has been amended 27 times, from the Bill of Rights in 1791 to the 27th Amendment in 1992.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-seven changes in more than two centuries.

img.title: TWENTY-SEVEN AMENDMENTS
img.tip: The Constitution has been amended 27 times.
img.scene: A row of twenty-seven small framed panels lining a marble hallway wall, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is the Bill of Rights?
questions.correctAnswer: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
distractors: The first seven articles of the Constitution
A list of duties for the President
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights is the name for the first ten amendments, ratified in 1791 to protect individual liberties.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bill of Rights = amendments one through ten.

img.title: THE BILL OF RIGHTS
img.tip: The first ten amendments protect individual liberties.
img.scene: Ten stone tablets arranged in two rows on a marble wall, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Why was the Bill of Rights added to the Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: To guarantee individual liberties and calm fears of an overly powerful federal government
distractors: To give the President more power over the states
To set the number of Supreme Court justices
To choose the nation's capital city
questions.explanation: Many states demanded a bill of rights as the price of ratification; the first ten amendments limit federal power and protect personal freedoms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Bill of Rights was the people's safety lock.

img.title: WHY A BILL OF RIGHTS?
img.tip: It was added to protect liberty and limit federal power.
img.scene: A large brass padlock and key resting beside an open book of rights on a desk, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is the separation of powers?
questions.correctAnswer: Dividing government power among legislative, executive, and judicial branches so no one branch controls everything
distractors: Letting each state print its own money
Giving the military its own branch of Congress
questions.explanation: The Constitution separates power among Congress, the President, and the courts so that each branch has its own job and limits.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three branches, three jobs, shared control.

img.title: SEPARATION OF POWERS
img.tip: Power is split among three branches with separate jobs.
img.scene: A sturdy three-legged stool standing on a stone floor, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of checks and balances?
questions.correctAnswer: The President vetoes a bill passed by Congress
distractors: A state sets its own speed limits
questions.explanation: The veto lets the executive branch check the legislative branch. Congress can answer with a two-thirds override - the system balances itself.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A veto is one branch checking another.

img.title: CHECKS AND BALANCES
img.tip: Each branch can limit the others - that is the balance.
img.scene: A balanced beam scale with three equal stone weights resting level, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is federalism?
questions.correctAnswer: A system dividing power between a national government and state governments
distractors: Rule by a single national government with no states
A plan giving all power to county governments
An alliance of separate nations for trade only
questions.explanation: Federalism splits authority: the national government handles matters like defense and currency, while states handle schools, roads, and local police.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two levels of government share the work.

img.title: FEDERALISM
img.tip: National and state governments share power in a federal system.
img.scene: Two interlocking stone rings of different sizes standing upright on a plaza, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What does the Supremacy Clause establish?
questions.correctAnswer: Federal law and the Constitution override conflicting state laws
distractors: State laws always override federal laws
The Supreme Court may write new laws
Governors may ignore federal court rulings
questions.explanation: Article VI says the Constitution and laws made under it are supreme; when a valid federal law and a state law conflict, the federal law prevails.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In a real conflict, federal law wins.

img.title: THE SUPREMACY CLAUSE
img.tip: Valid federal law beats a conflicting state law.
img.scene: A tall lighthouse beam shining over a harbor while smaller lamps glow below, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which branch of the federal government does Article III of the Constitution create?
questions.correctAnswer: The judicial branch - the federal courts
questions.explanation: Article I creates Congress, Article II the presidency, and Article III the judicial branch headed by the Supreme Court.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article Three builds the courts.

img.title: ARTICLE III: THE COURTS
img.tip: Article III establishes the federal judicial branch.
img.scene: A marble courthouse with tall columns and wide steps under a clear sky, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: The legislative branch of the federal government is called Congress. What two chambers make it up?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate and the House of Representatives
distractors: The Cabinet and the Supreme Court
The House of Lords and the House of Commons
questions.explanation: Congress is bicameral: a Senate with equal state representation and a House apportioned by population.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two chambers, one Congress.

img.title: TWO CHAMBERS
img.tip: Congress = the Senate plus the House of Representatives.
img.scene: A grand domed capitol building with two long wings extending on both sides, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many senators does each state send to the U.S. Senate?
questions.correctAnswer: Two senators per state
distractors: It depends on the state's population
questions.explanation: Equal representation in the Senate was the small states' win in the Great Compromise: two senators per state, 100 in all.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Big state or small state - two senators each.

img.title: TWO PER STATE
img.tip: Every state elects exactly two U.S. senators.
img.scene: Two tall chairs standing side by side on a raised platform in a semicircular chamber, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How are seats in the U.S. House of Representatives divided among the states?
questions.correctAnswer: By population, counted in the census - 435 seats in total
distractors: Equally - the same number for every state
By how long the state has been in the Union
questions.explanation: House seats follow population. After each ten-year census, the 435 seats are reapportioned among the states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: More people, more House seats.

img.title: SEATS BY POPULATION
img.tip: The House's 435 seats are apportioned by population.
img.scene: A large semicircular chamber filled with many rows of desks and chairs, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How long is one term for a U.S. senator?
questions.correctAnswer: Six years
questions.explanation: Senators serve six-year terms, staggered so that about one third of the Senate is elected every two years.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senators get the long six-year runway.

img.title: SIX-YEAR SENATE TERMS
img.tip: A U.S. senator serves a six-year term.
img.scene: A long calendar ribbon stretching across a desk with six marked sections, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How long is one term for a member of the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.correctAnswer: Two years
questions.explanation: House members serve two-year terms, keeping the House closely answerable to voters - the whole House is up for election every two years.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House members face the voters every two years.

img.title: TWO-YEAR HOUSE TERMS
img.tip: A U.S. representative serves a two-year term.
img.scene: A short calendar ribbon with two marked sections lying on a desk, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the main steps for a federal bill to become a law?
questions.correctAnswer: Introduced in Congress, passed by both chambers, then signed by the President
distractors: Signed by the President, then introduced in Congress
Approved by the Supreme Court, then voted on by states
Written by a governor, then passed by the Senate only
questions.explanation: A bill must pass the House and Senate in identical form and then be signed by the President (or survive a veto override) to become law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Both chambers first, the President last.

img.title: HOW A BILL BECOMES LAW
img.tip: Congress passes it in both chambers; the President signs it.
img.scene: A rolled scroll traveling along a path past two chamber doors toward a large wooden desk, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: If the President vetoes a bill, how can Congress still make it law?
questions.correctAnswer: By overriding the veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate
distractors: By asking the Supreme Court to sign it
By passing it again with a simple majority
By sending it to the state governors
questions.explanation: A two-thirds vote in each chamber overrides a presidential veto - one of the Constitution's key checks and balances.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds in both chambers beats a veto.

img.title: OVERRIDING A VETO
img.tip: Congress can override a veto with two-thirds of both chambers.
img.scene: A large wooden door being pushed open by many hands working together, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which power belongs to Congress alone?
questions.correctAnswer: Declaring war
distractors: Commanding troops in battle day to day
questions.explanation: Only Congress may declare war. The President commands the armed forces, courts interpret law, and pardons belong to the President.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: War is declared by Congress, not the President.

img.title: ONLY CONGRESS DECLARES WAR
img.tip: The power to declare war belongs to Congress alone.
img.scene: A solemn assembly hall with rows of legislators seated in debate, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How long is one term for the President of the United States?
questions.correctAnswer: Four years
questions.explanation: The President serves a four-year term and, under the 22nd Amendment, may be elected only twice.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four years per presidential term.

img.title: FOUR-YEAR PRESIDENTIAL TERM
img.tip: A president serves four years per term.
img.scene: A white government mansion with columns and a green lawn under a bright sky, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What did the 22nd Amendment do?
questions.correctAnswer: Limited the President to two elected terms
distractors: Gave women the right to vote
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections, the 22nd Amendment caps a president at two elected terms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two terms and done - that is the 22nd.

img.title: THE 22ND AMENDMENT
img.tip: Presidents are limited to two elected terms.
img.scene: Two stone pillars standing side by side at the entrance of a government building, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: The President is called the commander in chief. Of what?
questions.correctAnswer: The United States armed forces
questions.explanation: Article II makes the President commander in chief of the Army, Navy, and other federal forces - civilian control of the military.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A civilian president commands the military.

img.title: COMMANDER IN CHIEF
img.tip: The President commands the armed forces.
img.scene: Rows of uniformed service members standing in formation on a parade ground at sunrise, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: A President refuses to sign a bill and sends it back to Congress with objections. What is this power called?
questions.correctAnswer: A veto
questions.explanation: The veto is the President's power to reject a bill passed by Congress; Congress may override with two-thirds of both chambers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Veto means 'I forbid' - the President's no.

img.title: THE VETO
img.tip: A veto sends a bill back to Congress unsigned.
img.scene: A hand holding a large pen above an unsigned scroll on a polished desk, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: The President nominates a Supreme Court justice. What must happen before that person takes the seat?
questions.correctAnswer: The Senate must confirm the nomination
distractors: The House must confirm the nomination
The Chief Justice must swear in a family member instead
questions.explanation: Under the advice-and-consent clause, the Senate holds hearings and votes to confirm presidential appointments to the courts and Cabinet.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate.

img.title: ADVICE AND CONSENT
img.tip: The Senate confirms the President's nominees.
img.scene: A semicircular hearing room with a long curved desk and a single chair facing it, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many electors are there in the Electoral College?
questions.correctAnswer: 538 electors
questions.explanation: The Electoral College has 538 electors: 435 for the House, 100 for the Senate, and 3 for Washington, D.C., under the 23rd Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 435 + 100 + 3 = 538 electors.

img.title: 538 ELECTORS
img.tip: The Electoral College is made up of 538 electors.
img.scene: A large hall filled with many rows of chairs facing a stage, seen from above, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many electoral votes must a candidate win to become President?
questions.correctAnswer: 270 electoral votes
distractors: A simple majority of the popular vote only
questions.explanation: A candidate needs a majority of the 538 electoral votes - 270 - to win the presidency outright.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 270 is the magic number in November.

img.title: 270 TO WIN
img.tip: Winning the presidency takes 270 electoral votes.
img.scene: A finish line ribbon stretched across a road with a trophy standing beyond it, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The U.S. Supreme Court is the nation's highest court; its decisions on the Constitution are final.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every appeal road ends at the Supreme Court.

img.title: THE HIGHEST COURT
img.tip: The Supreme Court is the final word on the Constitution.
img.scene: A grand marble courthouse with tall columns at the top of a wide staircase, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is judicial review?
questions.correctAnswer: The power of the courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution
distractors: The power of Congress to remove judges at will
The President's review of court budgets
A yearly inspection of courthouse buildings
questions.explanation: Established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), judicial review lets courts declare laws unconstitutional - a core check on the other branches.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Courts can strike down laws that break the Constitution.

img.title: JUDICIAL REVIEW
img.tip: Courts may strike down laws that violate the Constitution.
img.scene: A judge's gavel resting beside a thick law book with a bookmark, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: How many justices sit on the U.S. Supreme Court?
questions.correctAnswer: Nine justices
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court has nine justices - one Chief Justice and eight Associate Justices. The number is set by Congress, not the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nine justices, one of them Chief.

img.title: NINE JUSTICES
img.tip: The Supreme Court has nine justices.
img.scene: Nine tall chairs arranged in a row behind a long wooden bench in a courtroom, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Why do federal judges serve for life during good behavior?
questions.correctAnswer: So they can decide cases independently, without fear of political pressure
distractors: So they never have to learn new laws
Because the Constitution forbids all elections
So the President can control them longer
questions.explanation: Life tenure insulates judges from voters and politicians, protecting independent judgment; they can still be removed by impeachment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life terms keep judges independent, not popular.

img.title: WHY LIFE TERMS?
img.tip: Life tenure protects judges from political pressure.
img.scene: A marble pillar standing straight and unmoved while storm clouds pass behind it, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What is the main job of the judicial branch?
questions.correctAnswer: To interpret the laws and the Constitution
distractors: To write and pass new laws
To enforce the laws with the military
questions.explanation: Courts interpret what laws mean and whether they fit the Constitution; Congress makes laws and the President enforces them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress writes, the President enforces, courts interpret.

img.title: INTERPRETING THE LAW
img.tip: The judicial branch interprets laws and the Constitution.
img.scene: A magnifying glass held over an open law book on a wooden bench, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which freedoms does the First Amendment protect?
questions.correctAnswer: Speech, religion, the press, assembly, and petition
distractors: The press, arms, and housing soldiers
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects five freedoms: religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms live in the First Amendment.

img.title: FIVE FIRST AMENDMENT FREEDOMS
img.tip: Speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition are protected.
img.scene: Citizens speaking, reading newspapers, and gathering peacefully in a town square, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What right does the Second Amendment protect?
questions.correctAnswer: The right of the people to keep and bear arms
distractors: The right to a speedy trial
The right to vote at age 18
questions.explanation: The Second Amendment protects the people's right to keep and bear arms, in the context of a well-regulated militia.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amendment two covers arms.

img.title: THE SECOND AMENDMENT
img.tip: It protects the right to keep and bear arms.
img.scene: A colonial-era musket and powder horn displayed in a museum glass case, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What does the Fourth Amendment protect citizens against?
questions.correctAnswer: Unreasonable searches and seizures by the government
distractors: Having to house soldiers at home
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment requires warrants based on probable cause and protects people and their homes from unreasonable searches.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no rummaging through your home.

img.title: THE FOURTH AMENDMENT
img.tip: It guards against unreasonable searches and seizures.
img.scene: A closed front door of a house with a sturdy lock and a welcome mat, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: A witness in court refuses to answer a question because the answer would admit a crime. Which amendment protects this right?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment protects against self-incrimination - 'pleading the Fifth' - and also guarantees due process and grand jury indictment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth lets you stay silent about yourself.

img.title: PLEADING THE FIFTH
img.tip: The Fifth Amendment protects against self-incrimination.
img.scene: An empty witness chair in a courtroom with a beam of light falling on it, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What does the Sixth Amendment guarantee to people accused of crimes?
questions.correctAnswer: A speedy, public trial and the help of a lawyer
distractors: Bail in every case no matter the crime
A trial held in secret for safety
Freedom from all punishment if poor
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, and the assistance of counsel for the defense.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fast, public, and with a lawyer - that is the Sixth.

img.title: THE SIXTH AMENDMENT
img.tip: Accused people get a speedy public trial and a lawyer.
img.scene: A courtroom with a jury box, a judge's bench, and a clock on the wall, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What does the Eighth Amendment prohibit?
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment bans excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Punishment must fit within humane limits.

img.title: THE EIGHTH AMENDMENT
img.tip: It bans excessive bail and cruel, unusual punishment.
img.scene: A set of prison cell bars with soft daylight shining through them, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What did the 13th Amendment accomplish?
questions.correctAnswer: It abolished slavery in the United States
distractors: It gave women the right to vote
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1865 after the Civil War, the 13th Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for a crime.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1865 - the 13th ended slavery in law.

img.title: THE 13TH AMENDMENT
img.tip: It abolished slavery throughout the United States.
img.scene: A pair of broken iron chains lying open on the ground at sunrise, symbolic historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: What two big guarantees does the 14th Amendment give?
questions.correctAnswer: Citizenship for people born or naturalized in the U.S., and equal protection of the laws
distractors: Free public education and free health care
The vote for women and the end of poll taxes

questions.question: How do Illinois judges reach the bench, and how long is an Illinois Supreme Court justice's term?
questions.correctAnswer: They are elected by the voters, and supreme court justices serve ten-year terms
distractors: They are appointed for life by the Governor
They are appointed by the President for six-year terms
They are chosen by the General Assembly each year
questions.explanation: Illinois breaks with the federal model: its judges are elected. Supreme and appellate judges serve ten-year terms, circuit judges six, and voters decide retention after the first term.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal judges are appointed for life; Illinois judges face voters.

img.title: ELECTED JUDGES
img.tip: Illinois judges are elected; top justices serve ten years.

questions.question: Which Illinois courts hear most trials - the first stop for most cases?
questions.correctAnswer: The circuit courts
questions.explanation: Illinois has a unified court system: circuit courts are the trial courts of general jurisdiction, the Appellate Court reviews their decisions, and the state Supreme Court stands at the top.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trials start in the circuit courts.

img.title: CIRCUIT COURTS
img.tip: Most Illinois trials happen in the circuit courts.

questions.question: How many counties does Illinois have?
questions.correctAnswer: 102 counties
questions.explanation: Illinois is divided into 102 counties, each with a county seat and a county board - Cook County, holding Chicago, is by far the most populous.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 102 counties tile the map of Illinois.

img.title: 102 COUNTIES
img.tip: Illinois is divided into 102 counties.
img.scene: A map in the tall vertical outline shape of the state of Illinois, divided into many small county regions filled with different soft colors, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: Which Illinois county is the most populous, and which city anchors it?
questions.correctAnswer: Cook County, anchored by Chicago
questions.explanation: Cook County holds more than five million people - over 40 percent of the state - and its county seat is Chicago, the state's largest city.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cook County and Chicago dominate the state's map.

img.title: COOK COUNTY AND CHICAGO
img.tip: Cook County, with Chicago, is Illinois' most populous.

questions.question: Under Illinois law, a municipality automatically gains home rule when its population passes what size?
questions.correctAnswer: More than 25,000 residents
distractors: Every municipality has it from its founding
questions.explanation: Article VII sets the threshold: municipalities over 25,000 are automatically home rule units; smaller ones can adopt home rule by referendum.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 25,000 people is the home-rule finish line.

img.title: THE 25,000 THRESHOLD
img.tip: Home rule arrives automatically above 25,000 residents.

questions.question: Besides counties and municipalities, what other layer of local government serves much of Illinois?
questions.correctAnswer: Townships, which handle services such as road maintenance and property assessment
distractors: Districts run directly by the Governor
questions.explanation: Most Illinois counties are divided into townships that maintain local roads, assess property, and run assistance programs - a layer many states do not have.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Townships quietly keep local roads and assessments running.

img.title: TOWNSHIPS
img.tip: Townships maintain roads and assess property locally.

questions.question: Which feature belongs to the Illinois Constitution but NOT to the U.S. Constitution?
questions.correctAnswer: Home rule powers for municipalities
distractors: A bill of rights in the opening articles
An elected legislature with two houses
questions.explanation: Both constitutions have three branches, two-house legislatures, and front-loaded rights. Home rule for cities is an Illinois-only feature of the 1970 constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Home rule is Illinois' special extra.

img.title: ILLINOIS-ONLY: HOME RULE
img.tip: Home rule appears in Illinois' constitution, not the U.S. one.

questions.question: What is one protection the Illinois Bill of Rights states expressly that the U.S. Bill of Rights does not?
questions.correctAnswer: An express ban on discrimination based on sex
distractors: The right to a jury trial
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 18 of the Illinois Constitution expressly forbids discrimination based on sex in employment and housing - a protection the federal Bill of Rights never spells out in those words.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Illinois writes the sex-discrimination ban right into Article I.
